title: Nice to meet you
goal: Greet people at the right time of day, say your name, ask how someone is, and understand why Arabic has no word for "is".
bekal: greet with *as-salaamu 'alaikum* and answer it correctly
say your name and ask someone else's — in the right form for a man and for a woman
build complete sentences without a single verb

dialogs.title: حِوَار — فِي مَعْهَدِ اللُّغَةِ
dialogs.intro: First day at a language institute in Cairo. Two people are sitting side by side in the waiting room.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Good morning. My name is Budi. And you?
lines.literal: morning the-light. name-my Budi. and you?

lines.speaker: أَحْمَد:
lines.id: I'm Ahmad. Nice to meet you!

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Nice to meet you. How are you?

lines.speaker: أَحْمَد:
lines.literal: with goodness, the praise to God. and you?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: نَعَمْ، أَنَا طَالِبٌ جَدِيدٌ مِنْ إِنْدُونِيسِيَا.
lines.baca: na'am, anaa ṭaalibun jadiidun min Induuniisiyaa.
lines.id: Yes, I'm a new student from Indonesia.
lines.literal: yes, I student new from Indonesia.

notes: **A greeting for any time of day.** اَلسَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ works morning, noon and night, to one person or to a hundred. Note that "you" (عَلَيْكُمْ) stays plural even when you greet just one person — that is not a mistake, it is the standard form. Answering it is not optional but a social duty: ignoring a *salaam* feels far ruder than ignoring a "hello".

**A morning greeting gets a different word back.** You don't answer صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ ("morning of goodness") by repeating it, but with صَبَاحُ النُّورِ ("morning of light"). In the same way, مَسَاءُ الْخَيْرِ is answered with مَسَاءُ النُّورِ. Echoing the same phrase instantly marks you as a foreigner.

**مَا اسْمُكَ is read *masmuka*, not *maa ismuka*.** The alif of اِسْم is a *hamzat al-waṣl* — an alif that disappears as soon as a word comes before it. You'll meet it everywhere: بِسْمِ اللهِ is read *bismillaah*, not *bi ismi Allaah*.

**اِسْمُكَ or اِسْمُكِ — choose by who you're talking to.** To a man: مَا اسْمُكَ (*masmuka*). To a woman: مَا اسْمُكِ (*masmuki*). The difference is a single vowel mark at the end, and it is the number-one learner mistake — English "you" makes no such distinction at all. Getting it wrong is harmless, but it is instantly audible.

**تَشَرَّفْنَا literally means "we have been honored".** Not "I" but "we" — a plural used out of modesty, a bit like a polite "we" in formal English. Another common option: فُرْصَةٌ سَعِيدَةٌ (*furṣah sa'iidah*, "a happy opportunity").

**كَيْفَ حَالُكَ literally means "how is your condition".** The ending ـكَ is what attaches to a noun to show possession — and it changes with gender: حَالُكَ (*haaluka*, to a man), حَالُكِ (*haaluki*, to a woman). The answer is بِخَيْرٍ ("with goodness"), almost always followed by اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ.

**هَلْ marks a yes/no question.** English flips the word order ("Are you a student?"); Arabic simply puts one word in front: هَلْ أَنْتَ طَالِبٌ؟ The rest of the sentence doesn't change at all. The answer is نَعَمْ (yes) or لَا (no).

**أَنَا طَالِبٌ has no word for "am".** Two words, and that is already a complete, correct sentence. This is not a shortcut or casual speech — Arabic simply does not use a verb "to be" in present-tense sentences. Adding one would be wrong.

**طَالِبٌ جَدِيدٌ — the adjective comes after the noun.** Literally "student new", not "new student". That is the opposite of English, so watch your word order. Also notice the tanween ٌ ـ on both words — the adjective copies the form of its noun.

**أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا** literally means "family and ease" — it is short for a longer sentence: "you have come to family, and may your way be easy". The short form أَهْلًا on its own is also common and works as a casual "hi".

grammars.title: The nominal sentence — a sentence without a verb
body: This is the first sentence pattern you need to master, and its biggest lesson is what is NOT in it.
after: The pattern: **[the thing you're talking about] + [what you say about it]**. That's it. Nothing goes in between.
Notice the tanween ٌ ـ on طَالِبٌ and مُدَرِّسٌ: it marks "not a specific one" — like the *a* in *a student*. The first word is the opposite, always definite: a name, a pronoun, or a word with اَلْ.
Only in the past does a verb appear: كَانَ (*kaana*, "was") — but that's for unit 13.

grammars.title: Personal pronouns and their attached forms
body: Arabic pronouns come in two shapes: the standalone one used as the subject, and the one that attaches to the end of a word to show possession. You will use the attached one far more often.
after: There are no separate words for "my", "your", "his" — they all fuse onto the noun as one word: *ism* + *ii* = *ismii*, "my name". Think of it as a possessive glued to the end instead of placed in front.
Only one thing needs extra attention: **Arabic distinguishes male and female even for "you"**. It's a single vowel mark at the end, but it decides whether your sentence sounds right or awkward.

blocks.text: Notice that saying goodbye uses two **paired** phrases rather than repeating each other: the one leaving says إِلَى اللِّقَاءِ ("until the meeting"), the one staying replies مَعَ السَّلَامَةِ ("go with safety") — much like "see you" answered with "take care".

blocks.title: When to use the Islamic greeting, and when not to
items: اَلسَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ is the most common greeting across the Arab world, including at the office and on television. It is not just a religious greeting but a normal everyday one.

With people you know are not Muslim — in Lebanon, Egypt or Syria, for example — the neutral greetings that are always safe are صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ, مَسَاءُ الْخَيْرِ or أَهْلًا. All of them are polite and carry no religious weight.

blocks.text: These phrases are not grammar to memorize — they are emergency tools. Learn them whole now; understand how they're built later.
عَفْوًا works two ways: it answers a thank-you **and** gets someone's attention in the street ("excuse me"). For a real apology, use آسِف — a woman says آسِفَة (*aasifah*).

blocks.title: One sentence that changes everything
items: أَنَا أَتَعَلَّمُ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ. مِنْ فَضْلِكَ، تَكَلَّمْ بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ. — *anaa ata'allamul-'arabiyyah. min faḍlika, takallam bil-'arabiyyah.* "I'm learning Arabic. Please speak Arabic."

The typical problem when learning Arabic in an Arab country is not that people are unfriendly but the opposite: as soon as they hear your accent, many switch to English, thinking they're helping. This sentence stops that politely, and almost everyone will happily stay in Arabic.

items: You walk into a bakery at eight in the morning. You say to the baker: ____.

You're leaving your friend's house. You say ____, and he answers ____.
